readerTitle: When budgets shrink, who decides what's a luxury?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (기업 행사 기획사, 사내 UX 리서치팀) · 수치 없음, 일반 원리 적용
insight: 불황에 무엇이 사치품이 되는지는 상품이 아니라 고객이 정한다. 같은 서비스라도 고객의 필수 업무에 묶이면 덜 잘린다.
misconception: 불황에 매출이 줄면 가격을 내려야 한다. 우리 상품의 성격(필수품인지 사치품인지)은 정해져 있다.

factChecks.note: 구체적 통계는 넣지 않았습니다. '불황에 사치재 수요가 소득보다 더 크게 줄어든다'는 소득탄력성의 일반 원리로만 서술했습니다. 게시 전 경제학 정의 표현을 한 번 더 확인하세요.
7번 카드의 '경기가 회복되면 사치재 수요가 먼저, 크게 돌아온다'는 소득탄력성이 1보다 큰 재화의 일반적 성질로 서술했습니다. 특정 시기·업종 수치는 인용하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: When budgets shrink, who decides what's a luxury?
body: A downturn hits. In the same week, a client sends two emails. One pauses the annual team retreat "until things settle." The other renews the payroll service without a question.
Both are business services. Both cost money. The client sorted them into two piles, and the piles decide who gets cut first.

image.label: A manager sorting invoices into two trays
image.brief: 사무실 책상에서 관리자가 청구서를 두 개의 트레이에 나누는 장면. 왼쪽 트레이 라벨 "Must keep", 오른쪽 "Can wait". 오른쪽에 "Team retreat" 청구서가 올라가는 중. 따뜻한 플랫 일러스트, 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Your bookings just fell.
body: You run a corporate events agency. You plan retreats, parties and conferences. Clients are cutting costs, and next quarter's bookings dropped sharply.

options.text: Cut prices across the board to win bookings back
options.feedback: Clients didn't stop booking because the price rose. Their budgets fell. A discount gives up margin on the events they'd still buy, while the "can wait" events stay paused.

options.text: Build smaller packages tied to work clients must do, like sales kickoffs and new-hire onboarding
options.feedback: This moves part of your service from the client's luxury pile to the necessity pile. You give up some big, glamorous events, but you keep a place in budgets that survive.

options.text: Keep the offer as is and spend more on marketing
options.feedback: It protects your brand and prices. But more ads won't refill a budget line the client just froze.

cards.title: The cuts weren't random.
body: Look at which events got paused. The holiday party, the luxury retreat, the awards dinner. Look at which stayed: the annual sales kickoff and the training day for new hires.

The kept events are tied to work the client has to do anyway. Skipping the kickoff means a sales team without targets. Skipping the party means a quieter December. The client cut the **events they could live without**, not the cheapest ones.

cards.title: Income and demand, plus necessities vs luxuries
body: When a customer's income falls, demand for **luxuries** falls faster than income does. Demand for **necessities** barely moves. For a business, "income" is its budget.
So a 10% budget cut doesn't mean 10% less of everything. It can mean almost no change to payroll and a deep cut to retreats. Your sales follow whichever pile your service lands in.

image.label: Two lines: necessities stay flat, luxuries drop steeply
image.brief: 간단한 선 그래프. 가로축 "Client budget" 감소 방향, 세로축 "Spending". "Necessities" 선은 거의 평평, "Luxuries" 선은 가파르게 하락. 숫자 눈금 없이 개념만 표현.

cards.title: The same service can sit in either pile.
body: "Luxury" isn't stamped on a product. The buyer decides, based on the job it does for them.
A two-day offsite is a luxury when it's a reward. It's closer to a necessity when it's where the new strategy gets agreed. Same hotel, same catering, different pile.
That's why naming the job your service does matters more in a downturn than polishing the service itself.
cards.softwareNote: Software buyers sort tools the same way. The system that bills customers stays. The dashboard three people open once a month loses its seats first. Linking a feature to a daily, must-do task protects it.

cards.title: Now you lead a team inside a company.
body: You run a small research team that interviews customers for the product group. The finance chief asks every team to defend its budget for next year. To her, your team looks like a nice-to-have.
How do you make your case?

options.text: Explain why customer research is valuable in general
options.feedback: True, but general value is exactly what luxuries offer. It doesn't move you out of the "can wait" pile.

options.text: Tie each planned study to a decision on a revenue project, and drop the studies that aren't
options.feedback: You lose some work you enjoy, but what's left is tied to must-do decisions. That's the necessity pile, and it's the last to be cut.

options.text: Offer to do all the same studies with half the budget
options.feedback: A lower price doesn't change the pile. Thinner studies can also make the team look even more optional next round.

cards.title: Don't rebuild everything around the downturn.
body: Luxury demand falls fast when budgets shrink. It also tends to come back fast when they recover. If you tear down your premium offer entirely, you may not be ready when clients start spending again.
Some buyers' budgets also hold up in a recession. And pitching a premium service as a basic need can cheapen it. Shift some of your offer toward necessities; don't erase what made it special.

cards.title: In a downturn, customers cut by pile, not by price.
body: Concepts used: **necessities vs luxuries** (the customer sorts what they buy) and **income and demand** (luxury spending falls faster than budgets do).
**Try it today:** list your top three products or services. For each, write the must-do job it's tied to for the customer. Any without one are in the luxury pile.
